A data space lets organisations share da: A data space lets organisations share data without a central owner. Three things make that safe: knowing who someone is, deciding what they may do with which data, and keeping that decision apart from the data itself. The hub takes each from a published architecture, protocol or regulation; every card says which, and where the hub implements it.

The <ram>IDS-RAM 2026-3</ram> (October 2: The <ram>IDS-RAM 2026-3</ram> (October 2026) is a design space rather than a blueprint, built around the Dataspace Protocol and the Decentralized Claims Protocol, and it leaves the <dp>data plane</dp> outside its scope. Its predecessor <ram4>IDS-RAM 4.2</ram4> described layers and central components such as an identity provider and a broker. The <rule>IDSA Rulebook</rule> recommends decentralised data spaces.

The <bp>Data Spaces Blueprint 3.0</bp>,: The <bp>Data Spaces Blueprint 3.0</bp>, the final version from the Data Spaces Support Centre, sorts a data space into business, governance and legal building blocks and three technical pillars: data interoperability, data sovereignty and trust, and data value creation. Its <ac>access and usage policies</ac> building block asks for policies enforced during the sharing itself.
an ODRL policy on every offer and an app: an ODRL policy on every offer and an approved data permit before any data moves (<odrl>odrl-engine.ts</odrl>, <pg>permit-gate.ts</pg>).

It hosts the <dspp>Dataspace Protocol</dspp>, the <dcpp>Decentralized Claims Protocol</dcpp> and <dpsp>Data Plane Signaling</dpsp>, with <edc>Eclipse Dataspace Components</edc> as an implementation and a <tck>compatibility kit</tck> to test against.

Not a technical pattern. Regulation (EU): Not a technical pattern. Regulation (EU) 2025/327 sets up infrastructures and roles and leaves the technology to implementing acts: <mh>MyHealth@EU</mh> for primary use, <hd>HealthData@EU</hd> with a Commission central platform for secondary use, <hdab>health data access bodies</hdab>, <permit>data permits</permit> and a <cat2>federated EU dataset catalogue</cat2>. Two rules shape every architecture under it: processing happens in a <spe>secure processing environment</spe> from which only non-personal data may be downloaded, and questions go to the data <r80>instead of moving the data</r80>.

Its <fs>feasibility study</fs> finds the integration feasible; for health it says Simpl-Open can support EHDS2, with many requirements of the central platform <fs22>still to be assessed</fs22>.

Why this matters when there is a breach: Why this matters when there is a breach
In an ecosystem of many organisations a: In an ecosystem of many organisations a breach will happen somewhere. Whether the others keep trusting the data space depends on how far it reaches and how fast it is known:
<b>Contained:</b> a stolen session or ke: Contained: a stolen session or key opens only what its credential, permit and purpose allow, for as long as its token lives; no position in a network grants more (NIST SP 800-207, section 2.1).
<b>Data stays put:</b> analyses run in t: Data stays put: analyses run in the secure processing environment and only reviewed, non-personal results leave it, so a breach at a data user exposes no records (Art. 73(2), Recital 77).
<b>Stopped at the source:</b> an issuer: Stopped at the source: an issuer revokes a credential and every verifier refuses it, without a central switch; EDC re-reads the status list after at most 15 minutes by default. The access body can revoke the permit and stop the processing (Art. 63(3)).
<b>Known and reported:</b> the audit log: Known and reported: the audit log shows who read what, which a controller needs to notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours (GDPR Art. 33) and the people concerned when the risk is high (Art. 34); essential entities give an early warning within 24 hours (NIS2 Art. 23).
None of this prevents a breach. It keeps: None of this prevents a breach. It keeps one participant's breach from becoming the whole data space's, and that is what lets the others keep sharing.

The <dsp>Dataspace Protocol</dsp> (DSP): The <dsp>Dataspace Protocol</dsp> (DSP) governs how data holders and data users negotiate access to health datasets. The EHDS regulation adds <hdab>HDAB approval</hdab> as a pre-requisite for <permit>data permit</permit> issuance before contract negotiation can proceed.
